questions.q: Why does this lesson recommend loading the raw landing tables as STRING columns rather than casting types at load time?
options: Casting and validation belong in the staging layer, not the raw landing table, so a load failure doesn't block getting the data in at all
Snowflake cannot store any type other than STRING
STRING columns use less storage than NUMBER columns
COPY INTO does not support typed target columns under any circumstances
questions.explain: Keeping raw landing tables untyped keeps the load step simple and separates 'get the data in' from 'validate and cast it,' which happens in staging.

questions.q: What is the correct pattern for loading a nested JSON feed, according to this lesson?
options: Land it as a single VARIANT column first, then use LATERAL FLATTEN to expand it into staging
Convert it to CSV before ever staging it in Snowflake
Force it into a rigid typed schema at COPY INTO time
JSON cannot be loaded into Snowflake at all
questions.explain: The lesson's pattern is: land as VARIANT (flexible), then LATERAL FLATTEN into staging — not forcing structure at load time.

questions.q: What does TRY_CAST do differently from a plain CAST?
options: It returns NULL for a value that fails to cast, instead of erroring out the entire statement
It is faster than CAST but produces identical error behavior
It only works on VARIANT columns
It automatically deletes rows that fail to cast
questions.explain: TRY_CAST turns a bad value into a findable NULL rather than failing the whole staging build — useful for catching data-quality issues instead of blocking on them.

questions.q: Why does the lesson recommend keeping the CSV source in its own raw table rather than combining it with the SQL Server export's raw table?
options: The two sources don't relate 1:1, so forcing them into the same shape would misrepresent the data
Snowflake only allows one raw table per schema
CSV files cannot be staged using the same file format as SQL Server exports
COPY INTO requires every source to share one target table
questions.explain: The CSV and the SQL Server export are deliberately different, unrelated sources — keeping them in separate raw tables respects that rather than forcing an artificial merge.

questions.q: What is the practical difference between a raw table and a staging table in this capstone's layering?
options: Raw is loaded as-is with no validation and is disposable; staging is typed, validated, and business-ready
Raw and staging are two names for the exact same table
Staging tables cannot contain NULL values under any circumstance
Raw tables are only used for JSON, staging tables only for CSV
questions.explain: Raw is the disposable landing zone; staging is where casting, validation, and data-quality checks turn it into clean, typed, business-ready data.
